The prophecy is returned to sender. Somewhere, destiny loses a tracking number.

situations.TextKey: The dead are very specific, very angry, and surprisingly helpful.

Several brooms have organized a union meeting inside a closet. Their demands include better bristles and fewer heroic montages.
The brooms respect your paperwork and improve one of your procedures.
Nothing is solved, but everyone feels represented.
Behind a dusty desk lies a pile of forgotten equipment, misplaced forms, and one suspiciously warm stapler.

You leave before a handling fee can be invented.

A locked reading room hums behind a brass door. The sign says silence is enforced by old magic and older librarians.
You learn something powerful, although the silence leans on your lungs like a stack of ledgers.
The door remains locked. Somewhere inside, a chair approves of your manners.
A translucent borrower wanders between the shelves, still looking for a book due several reigns ago.
The search is exhausting, but the borrower remembers a trick from a very old appendix.
The notes are faded, useful, and faintly apologetic.
A shelf blocks your path. It appears to be sorting travellers by usefulness.

You win the argument, but only because the shelf runs out of brackets.
A book lies open on a lectern. The margin notes are arguing with the printed text and winning.
The notes teach you how to contradict reality with better formatting.
The book mutters that this will be cited later.
A reservation slip bears your name, although you are fairly certain you never reserved a destiny.

You pull out something useful. The slot keeps a small amount of you as a late fee.
A supply cart rattles into view, stacked with labels, keys, charms, and items that insist they are tax-deductible.
The cart unfolds into a shop with entirely too many small drawers.
You leave before the cart can charge you for browsing.
A narrow door stands between two shelves, labelled 'Definitely Not Here'. The label has been corrected so many times that the wood looks embarrassed.
The door opens into a corridor that has been waiting for someone with exactly your lack of authorization.
The door accepts this as a valid administrative category and stops being your problem.
The door sulks. The archive sends you somewhere more affordable.
A catalogue whispers your name, then several names that are nearly yours, then an annotation about your likely shelf life.

The chair judges your posture, your handwriting, and one decision you made six rooms ago.

A shelf creaks your name in a voice like old varnish. It offers to put one part of you somewhere tidier.

The soul leaves behind gratitude, a receipt, and a worrying amount of paperwork.
The soul settles. The ink warms under your hand.
The soul nods. It clearly expected this.

The book reads back. It has notes.
The pass is temporary, the shop is not, and the prices look almost reasonable.
The rope is surprised. Nobody respects the rope.
An ink well sits on the lowest shelf. The ink inside reflects the ceiling, then the stars, then a room you have not entered yet.

The footnote is unbearably useful.

Three witnesses swear you were here before. Unfortunately, none of them agree on what you were doing.
The witness produces something official from an inside pocket, and two duplicate notices from the other one.
One false statement leaves your file. A summons arrives to replace it.
The contradictions are useful. So is the protection they buy you — and so, unfortunately, is the witness now attached to your filing.
A sealed side door claims to lead directly to the right corridor. The seal disagrees in very small print.
The corridor is exactly as advertised, and so is the summons that was pinned to the other side of the door.
The ward is yours. Word travels: whatever is waiting has been told to take you seriously.
For one impossible minute, no one is responsible for anything. A cup of tea steams beside an abandoned ledger.
It tastes like dust, mercy, and exactly a fifth of your maximum health.
One genuinely useful correction, and one clerk's private arrangement about hours worked after the counter closes.
A filing cabinet opens helpfully. The other furniture watches it with professional suspicion.

The claim is accepted, at a rate that depends entirely on how quickly you finish the next piece of work.
A wall map shows three routes to the same office. Two exist only on Tuesdays, and one is arguing with itself.
You arrive early and unannounced. Nobody has authorised payment for work done off the route.
The annotations are useful and terrifying in equal measure. One of them turns out to be the wrong form entirely.
The creases cross out a corridor that was never there. You keep the map. The map keeps handing you the wrong form.
